llm.reply:
The phenotypic presentation of Marfan syndrome encompasses extensive multisystem pathology [1]. It represents an autosomal dominant connective tissue disorder arising primarily from mutations in the FBN1 gene [23: "multisystem connective tissue disease with autosomal dominant inheritance. It is mainly caused by FBN1 gene mutation"]. Clinical management relies on standardized diagnostic frameworks such as the Ghent II criteria to evaluate high-risk manifestations [25: "Ghent II Nosology of MFS criteria are crucial in MFS diagnosis, guiding clinicians in identifying high-risk patients"].

## Clinical Manifestations

MedGen lists these clinical features: Aortic regurgitation [8], Arachnodactyly [12], Astigmatism [16], Ectopia lentis [20], Esotropia [24], Exotropia [26], Pes planus [27], Glaucoma [28], Congestive heart failure [29] and Hypertropia [30].

## Disease Management

Current therapeutic strategies focus on early detection to improve patient outcomes [23: "early identification, early diagnosis, and early treatment can effectively prolong the life span of patients"]. Dedicated clinical evaluations target vascular pathology, notably through trials such as Losartan Versus Atenolol for the Treatment of Marfan Syndrome [17]. Longitudinal patient care relies heavily on systemic screening protocols [25: "screenings, assessments, and close follow-ups to optimize the continuum of care"].

The disease Marfan syndrome is associated with well-defined clinical manifestations [1]. MedGen lists these clinical features: Aortic regurgitation [8], Arachnodactyly [12], Astigmatism [16], Ectopia lentis [20], Esotropia [24], Exotropia [26], Pes planus [27], Glaucoma [28], Congestive heart failure [29] and Hypertropia [30]. It is an autosomal dominant disorder of connective tissue that primarily arises from mutations in FBN1 [23: "multisystem connective tissue disease with autosomal dominant inheritance. It is mainly caused by FBN1 gene mutation"].

## Clinical Evidence

Diagnostic assessment frequently relies on standardized criteria to identify individuals at elevated risk [25: "The Ghent II Nosology of MFS criteria are crucial in MFS diagnosis, guiding clinicians in identifying high-risk patients"]. Primary literature reviews include publication 2402263 [6], publication 35894201 [10], publication 37058316 [14], publication 38517496 [18], and publication 8733052 [22]. Relevant indexed biomedical titles include Marfan syndrome. [2], [Latest advances in the diagnosis and treatment of Marfan syndrome]. [7], What Is Marfan Syndrome? [11], Marfan syndrome. [15], and Marfan syndrome. [19]. The MedGen title is Marfan syndrome [3], and literature entities catalog Marfan Syndrome [4].

## Investigational Studies

Multiple clinical trials have evaluated therapeutics designed to manage aortic pathology across affected patient cohorts. Documented clinical trials include Studies of Heritable Disorders of Connective Tissue [5], Comparison of Two Medications Aimed at Slowing Aortic Root Enlargement in Individuals With Marfan Syndrome [9], Angiotensin Converting Enzyme Inhibitors in Marfan Syndrome [13], Losartan Versus Atenolol for the Treatment of Marfan Syndrome [17], and A Randomized, Open-label, LOSARTAN Therapy on the Progression of Aortic Root Dilation in Patients With Marfan Syndrome [21].
